title: Sudden Collapse and Unwell (Anaphylaxis)
patient_instructions: You are Jane, the adult daughter of Margaret (58), who has suddenly become unwell and is too breathless and drowsy to talk, so you are giving the history. You called an ambulance and were brought to this rural clinic. If asked, confirm your mother has previously said she is happy for you to speak for her. Story: about 20 minutes ago you were both in the backyard having afternoon tea; she suddenly said her throat felt tight, started breathing noisily, went pale and slumped. She may have choked briefly on food, but you also noticed she was gardening near the roses just before. She has type 2 diabetes and is on insulin; you are not sure if she missed lunch. She has hay fever. Only volunteer the insect exposure ('she was near the garden, maybe something bit her neck') if the candidate asks about triggers, insect bites, or what she was doing beforehand. She is not on any other regular medications and has no known drug allergies. Affect: frightened, tearful, keeps asking 'Is she going to be okay?' You want reassurance and a clear explanation of what is wrong. If the candidate is calm, explains the diagnosis, and treats urgently you become reassured.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor on duty at Young District Hospital (rural NSW). Margaret, 58, has been brought in by her daughter after suddenly becoming unwell and collapsing 20 minutes ago. She is too unstable to talk. Vital signs in the stem show hypotension, tachycardia and low oxygen saturation. In the next 8 minutes: obtain a focused collateral history from the daughter, generate a differential for sudden collapse, request a targeted examination from the examiner, state your provisional diagnosis and outline your immediate emergency management to the daughter. Address consent and confidentiality appropriately given the patient cannot speak for herself.
examiner_instructions: This station tests recognition and emergency management of anaphylaxis within a sudden-collapse differential. Reward: brief confidentiality/consent statement (emergency provisions allow gathering/sharing information to give urgent care); systematic differential (cardiac, neuro, respiratory/PE, sepsis/meningococcaemia, AAA, hypoglycaemia, anaphylaxis); asking trigger FIRST; early check of PMH, medications (insulin) and allergies; requesting bedside glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia. On examination reveal: drowsy, wheeze/stridor, urticarial rash, insect-bite mark on neck, hypotension. The candidate MUST diagnose anaphylaxis clinically and give IM adrenaline first-line. Prompt only if stuck: 'What is your single most important treatment right now?' Do not reward antihistamines/steroids as first-line.

criteria: Introduces self, confirms consent/confidentiality with relative and applies emergency provisions
Uses open question then explores super-acute 'unwell' (LOC, faint, pain)
Asks trigger first (new food, medication, insect bite) before aggravating/relieving factors
Screens key systems (cardiac, neuro, respiratory, infection) for differential
Elicits PMH, medications (insulin) and allergies early
Generates structured differential for sudden collapse
Requests targeted examination (conscious level, rash, stridor/wheeze, insect bite, vitals incl. SpO2)
Requests bedside blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia
Correctly recognises anaphylaxis as a clinical diagnosis from multi-system features
Gives IM adrenaline 0.01 mL/kg 1:1000 (max 0.5 mL) anterolateral thigh as first-line, repeat every 5 min if no improvement
Lays patient flat (legs elevated if hypotensive), does NOT let her stand/walk; high-flow oxygen, IV access and fluid bolus
Calls 000 and arranges retrieval; states antihistamines/steroids are NOT first-line
Post-event: observe >=4 h for biphasic reaction, adrenaline auto-injector, ASCIA Action Plan, allergy/immunology referral
Calm, empathetic communication with a frightened relative
Explains diagnosis and plan in plain language and checks understanding

red_flags: Acute onset hypotension, bronchospasm or upper-airway obstruction (stridor, throat tightness, tongue/lip swelling) - anaphylaxis until proven otherwise, even without skin features
Sudden collapse with crushing chest pain radiating to arm/jaw suggesting myocardial infarction or with tearing back pain suggesting ruptured AAA
Reduced conscious level / drowsiness with unstable vital signs
Non-blanching purpuric rash with fever indicating meningococcaemia/sepsis
Hypoglycaemia in an insulin-treated patient as a rapidly reversible cause of collapse
australian_guidelines: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline first-line 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 (max 0.5 mg adult), repeat every 5 minutes as needed; antihistamines and corticosteroids are not first-line and do not treat airway/cardiovascular compromise
ASCIA positioning: lay patient flat (elevate legs if hypotensive), do NOT allow patient to stand or walk (risk of fatal 'empty ventricle'); sitting only if breathing is difficult

ASCIA post-anaphylaxis care: observe minimum 4 hours for biphasic reaction, prescribe adrenaline auto-injector (EpiPen 300 microg adult / EpiPen Jr 150 microg child), personalised ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis and immunology/allergy referral
Call 000 for ambulance/retrieval; manage within DRSABCD emergency framework
Australian Privacy Principles / duty of care: in a life-threatening emergency where the patient cannot consent, necessary information may be gathered and shared to provide urgent care
learning_objectives: Formulate a systematic differential diagnosis for sudden collapse in an adult
Recognise anaphylaxis as a clinical diagnosis and treat immediately with IM adrenaline
Deliver ASCIA-concordant anaphylaxis management including positioning, adrenaline dosing and adjuncts
Take a focused collateral history while managing consent and confidentiality in an emergency
Exclude reversible mimics such as hypoglycaemia with a bedside glucose
key_points: Anaphylaxis is defined by acute onset HYPOtension (not hypertension), bronchospasm or upper-airway obstruction, which may occur even without skin features
Ask about the trigger early - in a super-acute presentation the trigger is effectively the aggravating factor
IM adrenaline in the anterolateral thigh is the single priority intervention; use the 1:1000 ampoule, not 1:10000
Never allow an anaphylaxis patient to stand or walk; lay them flat with legs elevated if hypotensive
In an insulin-treated patient always check a bedside glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia as a reversible cause of collapse

citations.claim: Anaphylaxis features include acute urticaria and angioedema of the face and airway, supporting recognition of the multi-system allergic reaction.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2030

citations.claim: Sudden-onset chest pain requires rapid evaluation with a 12-lead ECG, underpinning the myocardial-infarction differential in sudden collapse.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.351

citations.claim: Emergency management follows the DRSABC sequence with 'danger' addressed first - the framework within which immediate anaphylaxis treatment is delivered.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1345
